query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of copper (approximately 3–5 at.%) to the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will enable the in‐situ formation of a continuous, Cu‐rich lubricious oxide layer during sliding that reduces both friction and wear at elevated temperatures without impairing room‐temperature performance.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy that exhibits low friction at room temperature but develops higher friction coefficients and wear rates at temperatures up to 800 °C due to uncontrolled and nonprotective oxide formation.
generation.intervention: Minor alloying modification by incorporating about 3–5 at.% copper into the CoCrFeNi matrix.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed in ambient air under a constant load (e.g., ~1 N) at temperatures ranging from 25 °C to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The segregation of added copper to the sliding interface promotes the controlled formation of a fine, nanocrystalline Cu-rich oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the copper-doped regions preferentially oxidize to form a continuous and adherent lubricious oxide film. At room temperature the film remains thin so as not to affect friction adversely, while at higher temperatures (approaching 800 °C) the thicker, well-adhered Cu-rich oxide film reduces shear stress and resists abrasive wear, thus maintaining lower friction and wear rates compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the copper-doped variant will exhibit consistently lower coefficients of friction and reduced wear rates across the full temperature range (25–800 °C), as evidenced by the formation of a stable, lubricious oxide scale.
generation.baseline: Undoped CoCrFeNi alloy, which shows low friction at room temperature but exhibits increased friction and higher wear rates at elevated temperatures due to uncontrolled oxide formation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable during sliding contacts under ambient atmospheric conditions at loads on the order of 1 N, with temperatures spanning from room temperature (25 °C) to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal copper concentration and the kinetics of the oxide layer formation require further investigation, and the interplay of copper with the existing microstructure may introduce unforeseen effects under varying load or environmental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of sliding wear test specimens: one set of the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and a second set modified with 3–5 at.% Cu. Using a pin-on-disk apparatus, perform sliding tests at three representative temperatures (25 °C, 400 °C, and 800 °C) under a constant load of ~1 N in ambient air. Post-test, analyze the friction coefficients, wear rates, and surface morphology (via SEM and XPS) to assess the presence and continuity of the Cu-rich oxide layer.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (via real-time force sensors)
Wear rate (by measuring material loss and track profilometry)
Surface oxide composition and morphology (using SEM and XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the copper-doped alloy does not display consistently lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates across the full temperature range compared to the baseline alloy, or if no continuous Cu-rich oxide layer is detected at high temperatures, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Question: How can high-throughput computational screening be used to discover lightweight, precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys with high-temperature strength superior to traditional ferritic superalloys?. System: Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system (specifically Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5 and Al15Cr5Fe50Mn25Ti5 as successful cases). Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt% purity constituent elements, melted at least six times for homogeneity, followed by drop-casting; subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for 2 hours for specific characterizations. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 700 °C) at a strain rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; in situ neutron scattering from room temperature to 1050 °C; synchrotron XRD and TEM characterization.
